metadata.title: 高中英语词根记忆法 · 精选情景阅读
metadata.description: 10篇主题文章，每篇串联2-4个相关词根，8-12个核心词汇在真实场景中自然出现

life.title: A Morning at the Botanical Garden
life.passage: Last Sunday, I visited the **botanical** garden with my **biology** class. Our teacher, a passionate **botanist**, explained how plants form the foundation of all **animate** life on Earth. 'Every **animal** you see depends on plants,' she said, pointing to a butterfly dancing above a flower. We watched a short **animation** about photosynthesis — how leaves turn sunlight into energy. At the **zoo** section, a **zoologist** showed us how different species adapt to their environments. The highlight was seeing **protozoa** under a microscope: tiny creatures invisible to the naked eye, yet full of life. '**Biology** is not just a subject,' our teacher reminded us. 'It is the story of how everything living connects.' I left the garden with a new respect for the green world around me.

questions.q: What did the students watch to learn about photosynthesis?
questions.a: A short animation.

questions.q: What did the zoologist show the students?
questions.a: How different species adapt to their environments.

writing.title: The Writer's Journey
writing.passage: My grandmother was a **biographer** who spent decades writing life stories. Her study was filled with **bibliography** cards, each one a tiny door into someone's world. 'Good **literature** requires more than talent,' she told me once. 'It requires the patience to **describe** every detail until the reader can see it.' She showed me her **autobiography** — a worn leather notebook filled with her own story. 'I learned to **dictate** my thoughts into a recorder first,' she explained, 'then **transcribe** them onto paper. The spoken word carries rhythm that typing cannot capture.' Her **graphic** descriptions made history feel alive. Before she passed, she gave me a single sheet of paper: a handwritten **subscription** to the idea that everyone's story matters. 'You don't need to be **literate** in the academic sense,' she said. 'You just need to pay attention.' Now, every time I sit down to write, I hear her voice: describe, dictate, transcribe. Tell the truth.

questions.q: What tool did the grandmother use before writing on paper?
questions.a: A recorder to dictate her thoughts.

questions.q: According to the grandmother, what does good literature require besides talent?
questions.a: The patience to describe every detail.

senses.title: The Concert That Changed Everything
senses.passage: The first time I entered a concert hall, I was twelve. The **audience** sat in complete silence as the conductor raised his baton. What followed was a sensory explosion. The **visible** passion on the musicians' faces matched the **audible** beauty filling the room. I had never **inspected** sound so closely — each note had weight and color. 'This is a special **aspect** of live music,' my father whispered. 'It cannot be captured in recordings.' During intermission, I **envisioned** myself on that stage someday. The **advisory** note in the program described Beethoven's deafness: he composed music he could only hear in his mind. That fact struck me as the ultimate act of **sensory** imagination. As we left, I felt a strange **sensation** — not just happiness, but a deep **sensitivity** to the world's hidden beauty. That night, I decided to learn the violin.

questions.q: What struck the narrator as the ultimate act of sensory imagination?
questions.a: Beethoven composing music he could only hear in his mind while deaf.

questions.q: What did the narrator decide to do after the concert?
questions.a: Learn the violin.

movement.title: The River Never Stops
movement.passage: My grandfather was a man who never stayed still. His life followed a single principle: everything must **proceed** forward. As a young **graduate**, he left his village and followed the **current** of a great river downstream, believing it would lead somewhere meaningful. 'The river does not ask permission to flow,' he would say. 'It simply **occurs** — and in that flowing, it shapes mountains.' He built his career through **successive** small steps: a bicycle repair shop, then a small factory, then a logistics company. Each **procedure** was learned through trial and error. When I asked him about his greatest **achievement**, he pointed not to his business but to a photo of his children at their **graduation**. 'That is the only **currency** that matters,' he said. 'What you pass forward.' Last summer, we scattered his ashes into the same river. The water, as always, continued to move.

questions.q: What principle did the grandfather's life follow?
questions.a: Everything must proceed forward.

questions.q: What did the grandfather say was the only currency that matters?
questions.a: His children's graduation — what you pass forward.

create.title: Building Bridges
create.passage: Architecture is the art of making ideas **tangible**. Every **factory**, every bridge, every school begins as a thought — but turning thought into **structure** requires something more. My older brother works as a **construction** engineer. Last month, he showed me the blueprint for a new library. 'The **structure** must serve the people who use it,' he explained, tracing his finger along the lines. '**Structural** integrity is non-negotiable, but so is beauty.' The design was **perfect**: light poured through glass panels, reading nooks tucked into corners, a garden courtyard at the center. 'The hardest part,' he said, 'is not the **operation** of building. It is convincing everyone involved that the finished **effect** will be worth the effort.' When the library opened, I watched children run through its doors. The **fact** of its existence — a place where anyone can learn for free — struck me as the purest form of creation. Someone imagined it, someone built it, and now it builds others.

questions.q: What does the brother say is the hardest part of building?
questions.a: Convincing everyone that the finished effect will be worth the effort.

questions.q: What does the narrator consider the purest form of creation?
questions.a: A place where anyone can learn for free.

society.title: The Mock Trial
society.passage: In senior year, our **civics** class held a mock trial. I was assigned to defend a fictional character accused of a **crime**. My opponent, the **prosecutor**, was the most **popular** girl in school — and terrifyingly prepared. 'The **legal** system does not run on popularity,' our teacher reminded us before we began. I spent weeks studying **legislation**, learning the difference between **civil** law and **criminal** law, and understanding what **justice** truly means. On trial day, I presented evidence showing my client was the victim of **discrimination**, not the **criminal** the **population** assumed him to be. '**Injustice** anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere,' I quoted, borrowing Dr. King's words. The jury deliberated for twenty minutes before returning their verdict: not guilty. I did not win because I was clever. I won because the facts were on my side — and because the law, when properly applied, protects the weak as surely as the strong.

questions.q: What did the narrator quote from Dr. King during the trial?
questions.a: 'Injustice anywhere is a threat to justice everywhere.'

questions.q: Why did the narrator believe they won the case?
questions.a: Because the facts were on their side and the law protects the weak as surely as the strong.

mind.title: The Art of Remembering
mind.passage: My psychology professor began the first lecture with a question: 'What is **cognition**?' The room was silent. 'It is how you know what you know,' she answered, smiling. 'And today, you will learn to make that knowing last.' She taught us that **recognition** and **recall** are not the same thing. Recognition is seeing a familiar face and nodding. Recall is pulling a name from the depths of **memory** without any clues. 'The **sophisticated** mind does not just store facts,' she said. 'It builds connections.' She showed us her personal **notebook** — 40 years of handwritten observations. 'Every **notable** idea I have ever had began as a **note** in this book. Writing is not recording. Writing is thinking.' That semester, I learned that intelligence is not about having a good memory. It is about paying **conscious** attention — the kind of attention that leaves a mark. By June, I could recite 100 poems from heart. Not because I was smart. Because I had learned to care enough to remember.

questions.q: What is the difference between recognition and recall?
questions.a: Recognition is seeing a familiar face and nodding; recall is pulling a name from memory without clues.

questions.q: What did the professor say writing truly is?
questions.a: Writing is thinking, not just recording.

language.title: The Last Fluent Speaker
language.passage: My great-aunt was the last fluent speaker of our village dialect. As a **linguist**, she spent her final years recording everything: folk songs, recipes, lullabies. 'A **language** is not just words,' she told me. 'It is a way of seeing.' She was **bilingual**, switching effortlessly between the dialect and Mandarin, and she believed every child should be **multilingual**. 'Each **vocabulary** you learn,' she said, 'opens a new door.' She loved **proverbs** — those compressed packets of wisdom passed down through generations. Her favorite was an old saying: 'The tongue has no bones, but it can break a heart.' I did not understand it then. Now, as I study **linguistics** in college, translating her recordings into a **dialogue** between past and present, I understand. **Verbal** expression is the most powerful tool humans have ever invented. Words can wound or heal, divide or unite. My great-aunt chose to heal. Every **vocal** recording she left behind is a bridge — from her world to mine, from a dying language to a living memory.

questions.q: What was the great-aunt's favorite proverb?
questions.a: 'The tongue has no bones, but it can break a heart.'

questions.q: What does the narrator now understand about verbal expression?
questions.a: It is the most powerful tool humans have ever invented — words can wound or heal.

transfer.title: The Letter That Crossed the Ocean
transfer.passage: In 1943, my great-grandfather wrote a letter from Shanghai to his brother in San Francisco. The letter took four months to **transfer** across the Pacific, carried by a cargo ship that **transported** silk and tea. 'I **confer** upon you the duty of remembering,' he wrote in careful English, a language he had taught himself from a borrowed dictionary. The letter was **transmitted** through wartime postal channels, each stamp a small miracle. When it finally arrived, his brother held it with trembling hands. The **portable** piece of paper weighed less than an ounce, but it carried the weight of a family's hope. That letter set in **motion** a chain of events: my great-grandfather's **introduction** to an American sponsor, a visa application, a **journey** across the same ocean he had only written across before. 'A letter,' my father told me when I first read it, 'is the most **attractive** form of magic I know. It contracts distance and **abstracts** love into ink.' I keep that letter in a frame above my desk. It reminds me that the smallest act of communication can change a life.

questions.q: How long did the letter take to reach San Francisco?
questions.a: Four months, carried by a cargo ship.

questions.q: What does the narrator's father call a letter?
questions.a: The most attractive form of magic — it contracts distance and abstracts love into ink.

keep.title: Things Worth Keeping
keep.passage: When my grandmother moved into a nursing home, I helped her sort through a lifetime of possessions. She **retained** almost nothing: a photograph, a wedding ring, a worn copy of her favorite novel. 'We think we **sustain** ourselves with things,' she said, handing me a box of old letters. 'But what truly **maintains** a life is service.' She had been a nurse for 45 years. 'I did not save lives,' she corrected me when I praised her. 'I **attended** to them. There is a difference.' She explained that the **contentment** she felt came not from what she **held** in her hands, but from the countless small moments when she was **present** for someone in pain. '**Attention** is the rarest form of generosity,' she said. 'You cannot **retain** youth or health or time. But you can **preserve** dignity. You can **serve** joy.' She died three months later, holding nothing but my hand. I understood then: the things worth keeping are not things at all. They are the ways we show up for each other.

questions.q: What did the grandmother say truly maintains a life?
questions.a: Service.

questions.q: What does the narrator say is the rarest form of generosity?
questions.a: Attention.
